root_idea.summary: The root centers on lowering or bringing under control: contempt and derision in one branch, and subjection or manageable service in another.
root_idea.development: From the underlying notion of treating something as low or submissive, Form I develops the meaning “to mock,” while the causative Form II develops the meaning “to subject, render subservient, or make operate according to an intended purpose.” Related nouns denote mockery, a laughingstock, forced service, and obedient ships.

qac_form_accounting.reason: Inflected plural passive participle; presented under the singular participial citation form.
Quranic plural active participle; presented under the singular active-participle citation form.

senses.definition: To mock, scoff at, deride, or ridicule someone.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic construction commonly takes مِنْ or بِـ; reciprocal usage can express treating the other as ignorant or foolish in return.

senses.definition: To subject, bring under control, or render subservient or manageable, directing a person, thing, or natural force to an intended purpose.
senses.usage_conditions: In the Quran this is used of celestial bodies, natural phenomena, animals, ships, and other created things made to serve an appointed order or purpose.

senses.definition: To make a force prevail against someone, sending it upon them with overpowering force.
senses.usage_conditions: A result-focused causative use, explicitly applied to the wind imposed upon a people.

senses.definition: To invite or induce one another to mock, scoff at, or ridicule.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic occurrence has a reciprocal construction in which people encourage each other to engage in mockery.

senses.definition: Made subservient, controlled, or appointed to operate under command.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic uses describe created things, including stars and other natural phenomena, as operating in an ordered course under divine control.

senses.definition: Mockery, scoffing, derision; in the construction of taking people as objects of ridicule or laughingstocks.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic occurrences are in a context of derision. The occurrence in 23:110 is also associated with an alternative interpretation of subjection or forced service.

senses.definition: Subjection or forced service: a person made subject to another’s will.
senses.usage_conditions: This is the alternative Quranic interpretation explicitly recognized for 23:110, alongside the interpretation “mockery.”

senses.definition: Service or subjection: a person made subject to another’s will and available for that person’s purposes.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic occurrence presents human differences in provision and status as a means by which some people are made to serve or depend on others.

senses.definition: One who mocks, scoffs at, or ridicules others.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic form is a definite plural active participle referring to mockers.

other_classical_meanings.definition: In a reported extended usage, to put someone in a position he does not regard as his right, producing a kind of mockery.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A tropical or figurative usage reported in a traditional example.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To jest or speak playfully rather than seriously.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Reported in an idiomatic statement asserting that the speaker is telling the truth and is not jesting.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of a ship, to have a favorable wind and voyage, obeying the wind and running its course.
To compel a servant or beast to work or serve against its will without recompense, hire, or wages; to make use of it without payment.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The evidence explicitly applies this use to servants and beasts and to unpaid work.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A person who is mocked at, scoffed at, or made a laughingstock.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The form can function as a singular and, in some usage, as a plural collective.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A person or animal compelled to work or serve without pay; the word is also reported for one who employs such a subjected person or animal.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Applied especially to servants or beasts. The extension to the employer is explicitly reported as disputed, with another authority correcting it to the employed subject.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A habitual or frequent mocker of others.

other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A broader Classical Arabic nominal use; the Quranic occurrence under this vocalization is separately presented with the service or subjection sense.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A herb or leguminous plant identified in the evidence with the plant called سَيْكُرَان.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A rare regional botanical usage associated with Khurasan.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Ships that obey and have a favorable wind.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A plural nautical expression for ships making a good voyage.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To make a ship obey and run its course, with a favorable wind and voyage.
An occasion or cause of mockery, scoffing, derision, or ridicule.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: It may describe a circumstance or a person who becomes an object of ridicule.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A person who mocks, scoffs at, or ridicules others.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A secondary Classical Arabic agent use of the same noun.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One constrained or compelled, brought into subjection, and unable to free himself from the constraint.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A general passive-participial description of a subjected person or thing, distinct from the Quranic natural-order use presented above.

cautions: سِخْرِيّ in 23:110 is explicitly reported with two interpretations: mockery and subjection or forced service; the examples and senses preserve both rather than forcing a single reading.

The vocalized forms سِخْرِيّ and سُخْرِيّ overlap in broader Classical Arabic evidence, while the Quranic contexts supplied here favor mockery for 23:110 and 38:63 and service or subjection for 43:32.
